title: Reverse-engineering XLA's tile choice for the Triton fusion
why: The sawtooth is a compiler decision, so it is code, so it has a rule. This is what could be derived rather than fitted.

documented_constraints.rule: the tiling cost model counts memory in 32-BYTE SECTORS and penalises partial-sector stores
documented_constraints.source: XLA PR on the tiling cost model
documented_constraints.consequence: DERIVED: in f32[B,L,N,N,3] a tile [tb,1,ty,tx,3] writes a contiguous run of 3*tx floats, so filling whole sectors needs 3*tx = 0 (mod 8), and since 3 is odd, tx = 0 (mod 8)
documented_constraints.verified: 18 of 18 genuine tiles recorded in this work have tx in {8, 16}. Never 1, 2 or 4.

documented_constraints.rule: every tile size must be a POWER OF TWO, or EQUAL TO THE DIMENSION SIZE
documented_constraints.consequence: explains the two regimes seen in the data without fitting anything: tb in {4,8,16,32} is the power-of-two branch, and tb = B (seen at B = 59, 61, 63, 123, 127) is the equal-to-the-dimension branch

documented_constraints.rule: a tile is rejected when its load exceeds 1048576 elements
documented_constraints.consequence: a hard ceiling far above anything we see, so the 1536 we observe is a cost-model PREFERENCE, not a constraint

observed_budget.finding: the tile is exactly 1536 elements = 6144 B = 48 x 128 in 51 of 56 recorded cases
observed_budget.exceptions: the five tb=B cases (1416, 1464, 1512, 2952, 3048 elements) and three at B=140,141,143 which take 3072, exactly double budget

the_search_space.reading: Combining the sector rule with the 512 budget reduces the choice from unbounded to TWELVE discrete candidates. That is the main result: the sawtooth is a pick among twelve, not a continuum.

what_i_could_not_crack.question: which of the twelve it picks for a given B
what_i_could_not_crack.hypothesis_tested: that it minimises total lanes, ceil(B/tb)*tb * ceil(39/ty)*ty * ceil(39/tx)*tx * 3
what_i_could_not_crack.result: 36% (17 of 47), and the misses are 11 to 17% WORSE in lanes, so lane minimisation is NOT the objective
what_i_could_not_crack.partial_pattern: (8,8,8) appears when B mod 8 is in {5,7,0} and (4,8,16) when B mod 8 is in {1,3,4}, which covers the two dominant choices but breaks on 8 of 56 cases (B = 45,47,75,77,93,95,153,160)
what_i_could_not_crack.confound: my extraction takes the FIRST tile of each signature, and the two Triton kernels are not consistently ordered across runs, so some of those 8 may be the second kernel rather than the heavy one. Not disentangled.

attack_points.mechanism: tx must be a multiple of 8 only because the innermost contiguous run is 3 floats = 12 B, which never fills a 32 B sector
attack_points.attack: make the innermost run a multiple of 8 floats and tx becomes a free parameter
attack_points.cost: padding components 3->4 puts v2=2 into the element count, forcing width 4 for every B and killing the split protocol. Padding to 8 is worse still. So this attack costs the width lever.
attack_points.status: identified, poisoned by the width rule

attack_points.mechanism: the hard limit is 1048576 elements, so 1536 is a preference the cost model computes, not a wall
attack_points.attack: find the flag or the input that sets it; a different budget changes the whole candidate set
attack_points.status: not found in 79 flags of this build, nor in the docs; would need the XLA source

attack_points.mechanism: tb = B is legal and was taken at B = 59, 61, 63, 123, 127. In that regime the tile is a DETERMINISTIC function of B, so the re-tiling randomness disappears
attack_points.attack: find what makes XLA take that branch and force it; a tile that always equals the dimension has no selection sawtooth at all
attack_points.status: MOST PROMISING and untested. We do not know the trigger: those five B are all odd, but so are many that took a power-of-two tile.

attack_points.mechanism: the choice is among twelve candidates whose total-lane counts span about 17%
attack_points.attack: not an attack but a bound: the tile-selection sawtooth cannot exceed the spread over those twelve, which caps what is at stake

honest_scope: The sector rule (tx = 0 mod 8) is DERIVED from documented cost-model behaviour and holds 18 of 18. The budget of 1536 elements is OBSERVED, 51 of 56, not derived.
The selection among the twelve is NOT solved. Lane minimisation is refuted at 36%.
The mod-8 pattern is post-hoc and breaks on 8 of 56, and part of that may be my own extraction confound. It is NOT offered as a rule -- four post-hoc patterns have already died in this work.
All of this is for Rd=18.30, L=5, N=39 on one XLA build. The sector rule should generalise since it follows from the layout; the budget may not.
